articles.title: Security expert hails Trump's Greenland pact as a 'big deal' on par with Alaska purchase
articles.summary: Col. Grant Newsham says President Donald Trump's Greenland deal effectively neutralizes Russian and Chinese ambitions across North American geography.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's newly announced security agreement with Denmark and Greenland would block U.S. adversaries from establishing bases in Greenland and limit adversarial investments on the island, a move one security expert says limits China and Russia's ambitions in the region. Speaking on "Fox & Friends Weekend," Center for Security Policy senior fellow and retired U.S. Marine Col. Grant Newsham compared Trump's pact with Denmark and Greenland to the U.S. acquisition of Alaska in 1867. Newsham argued the agreement secures vital North American defense geography while limiting Russian and Chinese expansion. "This is a big deal. This is right up there with Secretary of State Seward getting Alaska," Newsham said Saturday. RUSSIA’S QUIETER NUCLEAR SUBMARINES THREATEN NATO, FORMER COMMANDER WARNS "It's a little different, because we haven't bought the place, but it locks up or brings into the fold, really, key terrain, key geography, up on our northeast," he explained. "Russia and the Chinese, in particular, they can't get in there militarily, and they cannot get in economically." On Friday, the president announced the deal in a post on Truth Social, saying the agreement would give the U.S. permanent control over security in Greenland. "I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns," Trump wrote. "There will be NO COST to the United States! At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America," he added. DENMARK VOWS TO DEFEND GREENLAND AFTER TRUMP REITERATES US SHOULD CONTROL TERRITORY Denmark and Greenland have emphasized that the agreement, which requires formal signatures and parliamentary procedures before taking effect, will preserve their "sovereignty and territorial integrity." RUBIO WARNS CHINA AFTER PANAMA SHIP DETENTIONS, CALLS HEMISPHERE SOVEREIGNTY 'NON-NEGOTIABLE' Newsham compared the move to Trump's previous foreign policy decisions, arguing the Greenland agreement fits what he sees as a broader strategy to defend the U.S. homeland. "Look at how the Chinese have been rolled back in Panama. And look what President Trump has done with Venezuela. You can see that there's a plan here for defending our homeland. And this really is a big deal, to put it in simple terms," Newsham said. TRUMP ENVOY WARNS CHINA'S POWER MOVE AT SEA IS THREAT 'WE CANNOT AFFORD TO IGNORE' Newsham said he believes the agreement gives Washington the freedom it needs to keep adversaries out of Greenland, though he predicted China and Russia would voice opposition. "They'll complain. They won't like it, but there's not much they can do about it," Newsham said. "They'll probably step up their activities in the territories they have up there. But nonetheless, this is a huge advance for the United States and our position." GREENLAND TALKS ON ‘GOOD TRAJECTORY,’ WHITE HOUSE SAYS AMID TRUMP TAKEOVER PUSH Secretary of War Pete Hegseth also highlighted the president's plans to expand the U.S. military presence in Greenland, reposting part of Trump's statement: "We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised the Greenland agreement, writing on X, "This historic deal is a huge win for the United States and the American people. Thanks to President Trump's vision and leadership, this historic agreement permanently guarantees U.S. security interests in the Arctic at zero cost to the U.S. taxpayer." "Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area. This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland," Rubio added.

articles.title: LA homelessness fraud cases expose deeper problem than stolen millions, oversight hawk warns
articles.summary: Rep. Michael Cloud says Los Angeles homelessness fraud cases expose a funding system that rewards program managers while keeping people in dependency.
articles.body: Federal charges alleging that millions of dollars were siphoned from Los Angeles homelessness programs are exposing what one lawmaker told Fox News Digital is a deeper failure in the way Washington funds and measures such programs. The latest cases out of Los Angeles fuel the concern of Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas that only are corrupt providers stealing taxpayer money, but that the programs aren't meeting their goal of getting people off the streets. "The only people really getting upward mobility in these programs, it would seem, is the people running the programs," Cloud told Fox News Digital after a House Oversight hearing examining federally funded homelessness programs in Los Angeles, Seattle and elsewhere. "And that’s not really what the program’s supposed to be about." articles.title: Tech industry scratches its head over Trump 'AI Force' proposal
articles.summary: Tech sector representatives say they view Trump's announcement as a response to growing public concern over AI's risks.
articles.body:
The tech industry is struggling to make sense of President Donald Trump's surprise announcement that he is creating an artificial intelligence task force and appointing a czar to oversee the administration's approach to the technology.

Trump, in a lengthy Truth Social post on Saturday morning, said he was forming the government body and would also soon name an AI czar to lead it. He offered few details, leaving members of the tech world unsure what the task force would do, who would be involved or how it would operate.

Four representatives for the sector, who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly, told POLITICO that the industry was not widely informed of Trump's decision prior to the Truth Social post.

"Nobody knows what the idea even is," one of the people said. Another said that feedback on the idea was not widely solicited within the industry.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Several of those canvassed said they view the move as a response to growing public alarm at the developing technology's potential risks. AI researchers at top AI labs in the past few weeks have issued stark warnings about the technology's power to destroy humanity, while executives including Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis have called for a slowdown so its risks can be adequately addressed.

"I think that he clearly feels pressure to say something, but he's torn because he's just spent the last few days saying that the whole thing is a hoax," Adam Kovacevich, CEO of the progressive tech industry coalition Chamber of Progress, said of Trump and his prior dismissal of AI doomsday scenarios

Since the departure of David Sacks, who stepped down as the Trump administration's previous AI czar earlier this year, the White House has been "making up AI policy as it goes," Kovacevich added. "I think it's clear they've really missed the presence of an organized leader like David Sacks was."

One of the tech industry representatives said they were confused about whether the task force would be charged with formulating more AI regulations or recommending policies that would further stimulate the tech's development.

Taylor Barkley, director of federal government affairs at the industry-aligned Abundance Institute, is eyeing it as a way to solidify a light-touch government approach to the technology he says will foster innovation.

"Any AI Force or AI Czar should have one job: keep the field open so entrepreneurs at every scale can compete, free from onerous regulation," he told POLITICO. "Existing criminal and civil law can handle bad actors. New permission regimes will stifle the very activity America needs most."

Trump's post Saturday showed a clear desire to keep the industry booming: "We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"

Trump's comparison of the new AI task force to Space Force led at least one tech industry representative to speculate that the proposal could be led by the Pentagon. "Rather than use civilian agencies to regulate it, use the Pentagon to try and dominate it," they said.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and NVIDIA did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the proposal.

Brendan Bordelon and John Hewitt Jones contributed to this report .

articles.title: Republican South Dakota secretary of state endorses Democrat to succeed her
articles.summary: "South Dakota deserves a Secretary of State who will strengthen confidence through performance rather than provocation," Monae Johnson wrote in a column publ...
articles.body:
South Dakota's Republican secretary of state urged voters to cast their ballots for a Democrat in the November election, arguing she could not back the GOP nominee — and drawing the ire of party leadership.

Monae Johnson announced she's endorsing Democrat Terrence Davis over Republican Heather Baxter, who defeated her in the GOP convention in June, at a moment "when I believe the integrity, stability, and professionalism of this office is at stake."

"South Dakota deserves a Secretary of State who will strengthen confidence through performance rather than provocation; who will support election officials rather than burden them for political effect; who will protect voter access and election security without pretending those goals are enemies; and who will treat the office's employees, voters, candidates, and business owners with dignity," she said in a column Saturday .

Baxter has campaigned as a staunch backer of President Donald Trump's efforts to reform U.S. elections and supports "robust post-election audits" and "improved hand counting methods," per her campaign website .

Baxter's campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Johnson wrote that she was endorsing Davis "with full understanding of what this endorsement may cost me" because he is the "candidate best prepared to protect the office and serve South Dakota with seriousness, steadiness, and integrity." She urged voters to "to look beyond the letter beside a candidate's name."

In a statement, Baxter told POLITICO her party affiliation was reason enough to side with her in the general election.

"In June, Republican delegates considered the record and nominated me over incumbent Secretary of State Monae Johnson, 59 percent to 41 percent. That was not confusion," she said. "That was self-government in action. The letter beside a name is not decoration. It tells voters what governing philosophy they will carry into the office that runs our elections and business services."

The Democrat thanked Johnson for her endorsement with a post on his campaign's Facebook account.

"Monae and I come from different political parties," he said. "We will not agree on every issue. That is exactly why her confidence in me means so much."

But Johnson's post was swiftly condemned by the state's Republican House speaker, Jon Hansen.

"South Dakota Republican Secretary of State, after being defeated at the Republican party convention in her reelection bid, is endorsing the Democrat candidate," he wrote on X . "Huge mistake! Do NOT hand our elections over to the Democrats! Vote REPUBLICAN Heather Baxter for Secretary of State!"

articles.title: Lawmakers see waste in DOGE’s ‘stupid’ $7B buyout costs
articles.summary: A new government report showing that the administration spent $7 billion paying staff not to work as it pushed its buyouts is sparking the latest round of scrutiny of President Trump’s DOGE era. A report from the Government Accountability Office (GAO) estimated the administration spent $6.7 billion on administrative leave after Department of Government Efficiency…
articles.body:
A new government report showing that the administration spent $7 billion paying staff not to work as it pushed its buyouts is sparking the latest round of scrutiny of President Trump’s DOGE era.

A report from the Government Accountability Office (GAO) estimated the administration spent $6.7 billion on administrative leave after Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) leader Elon Musk launched the buyouts.

Employees who took the buyout were paid through the end of the fiscal year, with some workers free from their duties for months on end while still receiving a paycheck as part of their deferred resignation.

The report issued Tuesday found that compared with 2023, use of paid leave in 2025 jumped 435 percent.

To lawmakers whose districts include federal workers from the D.C. area, the report is a referendum on Trump and Musk’s approach to the workforce in the name of efficiency.

“First of all, how stupid was it to pay people to stay home for four or five months — or longer — getting paid, and they don’t have to do anything, and we’ve robbed the American people of the services they were providing,” said Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), whose district of roughly 80,000 federal workers saw 20,000 lose their jobs early in the Trump administration.

“There are ways to be more efficient. There are ways to shrink the headcount, and DOGE did it in the absolute stupidest way.”

The report’s findings show an astounding jump in paid leave by almost every metric.

Salary costs attributable to paid leave jumped sixfold between 2023 and 2025.

Total workdays of paid administrative leave went from around 4 million before Trump to 21.6 million workdays in 2025.

And while in 2023 and 2024 just 600 federal workers across the whole of government took more than three months paid leave, in 2025 that number jumped to almost 100,000.

The GAO estimates that 144,312 federal workers used the deferred resignation program .

“I’m not surprised,” Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) said of the cost of firing people.

“We were saying that it makes more sense to keep the people who actually get rid of waste, fraud, and abuse in the government employed. It also makes sense to support our federal workers at a time when you know there’s a transition in government. Instead, they gave people this option and paid people not to work, and as a result, we’re going to see more reports like this come out, showing how much money was lost and how much taxpayer money was wasted.”

The Trump administration has defended the cost of the buyouts, noting that paid leave costs are akin to salary costs they would have paid for those workers anyway.

Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor noted that 270,000 federal workers have left government since the start of the Trump administration, whether that’s through the buyouts, layoffs or other methods.

The GAO’s report found the administration spent $9.5 billion on paid leave, though it attributed $6.7 billion to the buyouts.

“For the sake of argument, let’s charge the entire $9.5 billion to DRP anyway. It was a one-time expense. What did the taxpayer get for it? Using rough averages, the fully loaded cost of a federal employee is about $150,000 per year. For 270,000 employees, that is more than $40 billion in annual costs. These are not one-time costs, but costs incurred every year in perpetuity,” Kupor wrote in a blog post .

“So, for a one-time expense of at most $9.5 billion, taxpayers save more than $40 billion each year. That’s a 400+% annual return, and the outlay paid for itself in under six months.”

The White House did not respond to request for comment.

Critics argue the Trump administration is failing to take numerous other aspects into account.

The Partnership for Public Service estimates that 132,000 took the buyout . That with another 10,000 in layoffs and a combination of early and regular retirements contributed to an unprecedented 319,000 government workers leaving in 2025 — double the yearly average.

But the group also found that the government then hired 20,557 people to backfill roles of those who took the buyout, noting that those new hires “tend to come with less experience.”

“All the work that these people are doing. How is that work getting done? Have they contracted out any of that work, have they rehired people to perform that same work, which we know they have done?” said Andrew Huddleston, director of advocacy at the American Federation of Government Employees, the largest federal employee union.

“So you’ve got to net all that stuff out at the end to be able to prove any real savings over time, and it’s unclear to me that they’ve done that, or that they plan to do that. But even the sort of top line numbers that they’ve got here are, I think, shocking, probably to most Americans.”

Beyer said many of those who left had significant experience and institutional knowledge.

“We’ve seen again and again how stupid it is to take people that have been doing a job for 20 or 25 or 30 years, know it really, really well, and you force them out either DOGE and RIFs, fork in the road, whatever. Then you have to hire brand new people who don’t know the job at all, and usually it takes months or years to learn it and to do just as well,” he said, referencing a reduction in force (RIF), the process the government uses to carry out layoffs.

“They aren’t bad people; they just — they’re starting from scratch.”

Rep. Glenn Ivey (D), whose Maryland district has many federal workers, also said the cuts were made without any precision or insight into what programs were being cut.

Musk is “running around like a nut, waving a chainsaw around, and brought in all these people that didn’t know what they were doing or anything about the agencies where they were making these cuts, or anything about the programs and policies that they were undermining and killing,” he told The Hill.

“It’s probably one of the most egregious mismanagement enterprises I’ve seen in the government in my 50 years around this town.”

Subramanyam said he believed the report was a “conservative estimate” and that a more fulsome cost-benefit analysis would need to look at losses to programs and of expertise.

“A person who is working on food safety who gets a fork letter and they leave and then there’s a salmonella outbreak because they’re not there anymore — you can put a dollar figure on that. But how do you know the cancers you didn’t cure, or the diseases you didn’t prevent, or the wars you didn’t start, right?” he said.

“It’s going to reverberate for a long time, as well as the talent that we are dissuading from joining the federal workforce for years to come. A lot of people used to think of the federal government as an attractive job where maybe you get paid less, but then you can get benefits, get job security, and also do important work for the American people, regardless of who’s president. And what’s happening instead is now people may not want to work for the federal government anymore.”

DOGE has faced backlash over its other cuts, including to government spending more broadly.

Numerous reports have found DOGE consistently overestimated the amount of its cost-cutting efforts.

An August report from the GAO found the agency’s “wall of receipts” took credit for cost-savings measures already in the works when it was created, while “DOGE did not provide sufficient information to verify the method used to calculate 96 percent of DOGE-reported savings.”

Huddleston said the Trump administration has yet to make that case that DOGE lived up to its name.

“It was extraordinarily expensive to the American people, and it’s really unclear what it is that we got out of it. I don’t know that if you ask the American people today if it seems like the government is running more effectively or efficiently that they’re answering yes,” he said.

“It doesn’t seem that way to me. … It seems like the entire enterprise has been a colossal failure.”

articles.body:
After President Trump announced this week he was banning Politico, CNN and MS NOW from accessing the White House, the three media outlets reported Saturday their journalists were denied access to the executive premises.

White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) President Jacqui Heinrich called on the White House to “immediately” restore access to these journalists and said the action constituted a First Amendment violation in a Saturday statement .

“The implications extend beyond these organizations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future,” said Heinrich, who is Fox News’s senior White House correspondent and co-host of “The Sunday Briefing” on the channel.

“The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably,” she continued.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D), a frequent critic of the president and his administration, also condemned the move in a Friday social media post .

“This is yet another attack on the First Amendment from a president who knows he and his party of bootlickers are deeply unpopular,” he wrote. “Donald Trump can’t hide from his failing record, so he’s banning journalists he doesn’t like to keep you from hearing about it.”

The Democratic governor will join ABC News’s “This Week” on Sunday.

The president continued to downplay concerns this week about rising costs amid his administration’s ongoing military operations against Iran.

The national average price of standard gas was around $4.48 per gallon on Saturday, up from about $3.20 a year ago, according to AAA . Additionally, diesel prices were up to around $6.49 a gallon on Saturday, after hitting an all-time high earlier this month.

On Wednesday, Trump said at a rally in North Carolina for U.S. Senate Republican nominee Michael Whatley that these hiked gas prices were a “very inexpensive price to pay” for this conflict.

Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee, will join Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures” this weekend.

Republicans have expressed concerns that rising inflation could cost them at the ballot box this November, as polling indicates the economy is a top issue for voters headed into the midterm elections and Americans blame Trump for bad financial reports .

The president said on Thursday that he has a “big decision coming up” regarding the future of this monthslong conflict.

“Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It’s a big decision,” Trump told Axios , adding, “Anything could happen with me.”

Next week, the president is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping for highly-anticipated discussions in Washington, D.C., following the pair’s May bilateral summit in Beijing.

Trump will greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday following his address to the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York City a day before.

Mike Waltz, the U.S. Ambassador to the UN, will join CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday ahead of the body’s meeting.

Rising concerns about artificial intelligence continued to play into political discussions this week, after former AI company employees raised alarm about potential risks associated with this technology.

In a new POLITICO poll, 63 percent of surveyed U.S. adults said they believed that AI could one day destroy mankind. Seventeen percent of respondents said this result was “almost certain,” while others expressed less confidence in this outcome.

Democratic lawmakers and some Republicans have demanded more oversight and guardrails for this technology.

On Thursday, Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) called on the president to convene a bicameral special session of Congress to address the issue of AI.

“The safety of artificial intelligence systems demands urgent attention,” he wrote on social media . “The President should convene Congress at once to address it. This is not a moment for panic or despair. It is a moment for government to govern.”

Booker will join NBC News’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday.

Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about the potential threats posed by this technology. On Saturday, the president announced that he would appoint an AI “Czar.”

“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” he wrote in a Truth Social post . “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP. We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!”

Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, echoed the president’s warnings about competition with China on this technology.

“AI is the most transformative technology of our lifetime,” he wrote in a Saturday social media post . “America must win the race for AI and energy dominance. We cannot afford to fall behind China.”

The Republican senator is scheduled to appear on Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday.”

Additionally, several states are taking steps to impose restrictions on the development of new data centers amid concerns that the water and energy usage of these facilities.

On Friday, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) and Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) separately announced new requirements for data centers in their states.

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) said on Thursday he would “absolutely sign” a statewide moratorium on new data centers if a measure was brought to his desk. The Democrat will join “State of the Union” on Sunday.

articles.summary: The Trump administration began construction on a portion of the U.S.-Mexico border wall cutting through southwest Texas’s Big Bend region despite local leaders’ pushback against the project. articles.body:
The Trump administration began construction on a portion of the U.S.-Mexico border wall cutting through southwest Texas’s Big Bend region despite local leaders’ pushback against the project.

Customs and Border Protection (CBP) told the Associated Press Friday that installation of 30-foot panels was already underway along this portion southern border. The construction started earlier this week, with the agency posted a photo to its website appearing to show a crane lifting one piece of the wall into place.

Big Bend is located on the bend of the Rio Grande and is known for its mountain range, river canyons and desert landscape; it is also home to an eponymous national park . There are five total projects in the region, with the Hudspeth County project being called “Big Bend 1″ on CBP’s website .

CBP added that it is not planning to construct a wall in “Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, or the Black Gap Wildlife Management Area.”

A federal judge paused Big Bend projects 2 and 4 until the end of September to “allow for additional public engagement.”

Local leaders and residents of Big Bend have expressed concern that the border wall projects will infringe on landowners’ rights. They also fear its presence will diminish its national park, in turn, impacting the economy.

Clara Benson, the founder of the No Big Bend Wall Coalition, told the AP she had received reports of construction supplies moving into the regions, adding her group would “continue to fight for this land no matter what the outcome is.”

“We will continue fighting to the end,” Benson said, per the AP. “You talk to people in west Texas and they say even if they put it up, we’ll fight for them to take it down. So this fight is not over.”

Yolanda Alvarado, a local cattle rancher and regional director for advocacy group No Big Bend Wall, said , “Our livelihoods are threatened at this point. Not just landowners, but business owners, and not just Big Bend National Park …. it’s everyone in this region.”

In March, bipartisan sheriffs from five counties wrote a letter to federal and state officials opposing the wall in the region. More recently, outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn (R) urged federal officials to meet with stakeholders about the issue.

CBP did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

FBI Director Kash Patel said Saturday the agency used AI to stop half a dozen school shootings and upped its use of the technology by 605 percent since he took the position.

Appearing on Fox News’ “Saturday in America,” host Kayleigh McEnany asked Patel about a statement he made in March claiming the FBI had prevented a school shooting in North Carolina after triaging a “tip” through AI software.

“We’ve done it in North Carolina and about half a dozen other states to prevent school shootings since I’ve been in the seat,” the FBI director told McEnany. “AI, when used lawfully, is a critical tool to triage data. For far too long the institutional morass in D.C. rejected the advancements of technology.”

“I have increased the use of AI in the FBI by 605 percent,” Patel continued. “And what we’re about to do is work with our … partners and look at databases and collect information and get DNA and then get these threats back out to the field and stop people from killing children at schools.”

He added that his move to embrace AI within the FBI was not “a political mission” and criticized Democrats for not asking him about the technology during his Tuesday Senate Judiciary Committee hearing.

Patel accused the Democratic lawmakers on the committee of acting “like buffoons on Capitol Hill” in another interview on Fox News’s “Hannity” following his meeting with them.

The Senate Judiciary Committee pressed Patel over reports that he used taxpayer dollars to fund personal excursions — citing alleged expenses on “date night” travels with his girlfriend, sporting events and a hunting retreat.

Patel denied these accusations in a July letter to Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) in which he pledged he was “ fully compliant ” with agency rules.

The FBI’s use of AI also comes as tech industry leaders warn that its growth needed to slow down to allow for the implementation of necessary risk prevention safeguards.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said last week, “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.”

Amodei later suggested granting an antitrust waiver for AI firms so they could work together on a safety standard, which drew criticism from lawmakers — including Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), who said during Patel’s hearing there is “absolutely no world” where he would give these companies “antitrust exemptions.”

articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Saturday signed a legislation package aimed at safeguarding the state’s election process against potential interference in the upcoming midterm elections.

The Democratic governor, who has repeatedly warned President Trump’s administration would attempt to meddle in these upcoming elections, signed 13 bills in Los Angeles.

“Donald Trump won’t stop until he can exert dictatorial control over your free vote and disenfranchise millions of people this November,” Newsom said in a statement . “California will stop him at every opportunity.

“We have no bigger task than fighting to protect the right to vote from interference and meddling – the future of democracy is on the line,” he continued. “These bills today build upon the wall California has built to safeguard our electoral process.”

This legislation package includes measures to prohibit the seizure of ballots or election records before results have been certified and imposes a felony penalty on authority figures who direct their employees to interfere in the delivery of a mail-in ballot.

Another measure requires election officials to notify California’s secretary of state and attorney general after becoming aware of an effort to obtain election records or technology. This follows Newsom’s signing of a law in May that prohibits federal agents from accessing voter rolls or election technology without a court order.

State Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) commended the new legislation package in a Saturday statement and noted the U.S. Supreme Court’s recent decision to side with California and other blue states to block the Trump administration from imposing its proposed changes to mail-in ballot voting .

“But we cannot, and will not, let our guard down,” Bonta said. “I have sponsored and supported multiple pieces of legislation to protect our democracy, and I’m grateful that Governor Newsom and the Legislature have now acted to further safeguard the right to vote.”

Democrats have expressed concern that the Trump administration would attempt to interfere in the November elections, in which the Republican Party is fighting to maintain its majority in Congress.

articles.body:
President Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., poured an additional $5 million into the Texas Senate race, according to a new Federal Election Commission (FEC) filing published Saturday.

The funds were earmarked for Del Ray Media LLC, a Virginia-based political media company, for TV and digital advertising against the Democratic nominee in this race, state Rep. James Talarico.

This marks the super PAC’s latest contribution to a pricey ad campaign battle between Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton and Talarico as they go head-to-head in this competitive race for GOP Sen. John Cornyn’s Senate seat.

In an FEC filing published earlier this month, the president’s campaign funding arm gave Del Ray Media $10 million to fund two attack ads targeting Talarico’s campaign.

Paxton’s campaign has also received nearly $54 million from the GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund’s (SLF) Texas affiliate, according to FEC filings.

The state attorney general was significantly trailing behind his Democratic opponent on campaign fundraising at the end of June, with Talarico’s campaign reporting about $21.5 million in cash on hand compared to Paxton’s around $1.76 million available funds, according to FEC data.

The two candidates are locked in a dead heat in the polls with less than seven weeks until the November election. The Democrat posted a one-point lead on the attorney general in a Hill/Emerson College Polling survey released Thursday.

The Cook Political Report , a nonpartisan election handicapper, rates this race as a “toss up.”

Republicans have placed pressure on the president to unleash his massive campaign war chest for the midterm races as the party seeks to maintain its control in both chambers of Congress this fall.

Trump has pledged to spend between $400 million and $500 million on midterm races, saving the rest of the super PAC’s funds for the 2028 presidential election cycle. The president pegged MAGA Inc.’s total cash on hand at “close to a billion dollars,” but the super PAC reported $403.45 million at the end of July in FEC filings .
